question: Can bottleneck paths through a graph of local simplices reliably separate noisy, curved, and intersecting manifolds without explicitly estimating tangent spaces?

key_findings.claim: Largest-angle path distance (LAPD) lifts point samples to local d-simplices, weights adjacent simplices by dihedral angle, and measures the smallest possible maximum turn along a simplex path.
key_findings.evidence: The method builds radius-local simplices, a shared-face adjacency graph, and an infinity-path metric; same-manifold paths can chain through small angular changes while cross-manifold paths must pay an intersection-angle bottleneck.

key_findings.claim: A density-based denoising step is essential to remove accidental bridging simplices near intersections.
key_findings.evidence: Simplices whose kth-neighbor LAPD exceeds a threshold are removed before clustering; the theory separates within- and between-manifold LAPD only after this pruning while assuming the retained graph stays connected.

key_findings.claim: Under random sampling and regularity assumptions, the paper proves a high-probability gap between within-manifold and between-manifold LAPD.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.7 combines upper and lower bounds to show within-LAPD is asymptotically below between-LAPD when simplex scale exceeds noise and sampling terms and remains below an upper geometric scale, with probability 1-O(n^{-(d+1)}).

key_findings.claim: The theorem does not give the explicit curvature-dependent upper bound needed in highly curved settings.
key_findings.evidence: Immediately after Theorem 4.7 the authors note that curvature can force simplices to be much smaller, but omit a precise bound because the required chaining volumes are complicated.

key_findings.claim: Approximate infinity-path computation yields a quasi-linear implementation and the experiments generally favor LAPD on synthetic subspace/manifold and selected real datasets.
key_findings.evidence: The numerical section uses landmark/approximation machinery to avoid all-pairs quadratic work, then evaluates clustering accuracy, learned cluster number, noise, curvature, intersection angle, and runtime against locality- and tangent-based baselines.

key_findings.claim: The method trades explicit tangent estimation for combinatorial simplex construction and knowledge of intrinsic dimension.
key_findings.evidence: Every candidate d-simplex requires local geometric checks and the correct d is treated as known; performance can deteriorate when sampling is sparse, dimension is misspecified, or simplex connectivity fragments.

method.core_idea: Cluster samples from intersecting manifolds using angular bottleneck distance on a graph of local simplices rather than Euclidean proximity or separately estimated tangent planes.
method.mechanism: Construct d-simplices at a local scale, connect those sharing faces, use dihedral angle as edge cost, compute minimax path distances, denoise low-support simplices, and perform threshold or spectral clustering on the resulting affinities.
assumptions: All component manifolds share a known intrinsic dimension d.
Samples are sufficiently dense and approximately random on regular manifolds.
Intersection angles, noise, curvature, and simplex scale leave a nonempty separation regime.
Denoising removes cross-manifold bridges without disconnecting true components.
Approximate bottleneck distances preserve the gap needed by downstream clustering.

techniques.role: Encodes local d-dimensional orientation without fitting a tangent plane at every point.
Weights transitions between adjacent simplices by local orientation change.
Measures the minimum achievable worst angular transition along any path.
Removes sparse or bridging simplices before label recovery.
Reduces distance computation toward quasi-linear scaling.

evaluations.setting: Random samples from multiple manifolds satisfying separation, smoothness, and noise assumptions.
evaluations.metric: Within-manifold versus between-manifold LAPD gap and success probability.
evaluations.result: Theorem 4.7 establishes a gap with probability 1-O(n^{-(d+1)}) in a specified scale regime.
evaluations.baseline: Distance graphs that connect intersecting manifolds solely because points are spatially close.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic unions of linear subspaces and nonlinear manifolds with varied noise, curvature, and intersection angle.
evaluations.metric: Clustering accuracy, inferred number of components, and parameter sensitivity.
evaluations.result: LAPD is generally more robust than tested MMC and subspace-clustering baselines, including difficult small-angle cases.
evaluations.baseline: Local-PCA/tangent, curvature, spectral, and subspace clustering methods reported in Section 5.

evaluations.setting: Selected real-world clustering datasets and scalability tests.
evaluations.metric: Clustering scores and runtime versus sample count.
evaluations.result: The approximate implementation remains competitive in accuracy and exhibits near-linear empirical scaling in the reported regimes.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's exact and competing clustering implementations.

limitations: Intrinsic dimension is assumed known and common across components.
The main guarantee uses strong sampling, smoothness, separation, and retained-connectivity assumptions.
No explicit curvature-dependent admissible simplex scale is derived.
Simplex enumeration can still be expensive as local degree or intrinsic dimension grows.
Thresholds for simplex scale, denoising, and clustering interact and require tuning.
Real data need not be a clean union of manifolds with a single intersection geometry.
failure_modes: High curvature can mimic a cross-manifold angular jump and split one component.
Small intersection angle plus noise can eliminate the theoretical LAPD gap.
Denoising can either retain bridge simplices or remove legitimate low-density regions.
Wrong intrinsic dimension produces degenerate or uninformative simplices.
Sparse sampling can disconnect the simplex graph before same-manifold paths form.
Approximate distance computation can blur narrow gaps.
reusable_insights: For intersecting structures, lift points to local oriented objects before computing connectivity.
Minimax path costs are natural when one bad transition, rather than cumulative length, identifies a cluster crossing.
Denoising and connectivity preservation must be analyzed together rather than as independent preprocessing.
A scalable approximation should be evaluated on whether it preserves the decision gap, not only raw distance error.
open_questions: Can the curvature-dependent upper scale be made explicit and data-adaptive?
How can intrinsic dimension and the number of manifolds be estimated jointly with LAPD?
Can mixed-dimensional or stratified manifolds be handled without separate pipelines?
What approximation error guarantees suffice to preserve clustering labels?
How does LAPD behave under anisotropic, adversarial, or nonuniform sampling?

competitive_landscape.title: Spectral Clustering Based on Local PCA
competitive_landscape.difference: Arias-Castro et al. estimate local principal subspaces and weight a point graph by tangent discrepancy; LAPD avoids explicit tangent estimates by comparing adjacent simplices and uses a minimax path metric.

competitive_landscape.title: Large sample spectral analysis of graph-based multi-manifold clustering
competitive_landscape.difference: Garcia Trillos et al. analyze graph Laplacians and annular proximity graphs with angle constraints; LAPD instead proves separation for an angular bottleneck metric on simplex paths and adds a denoising stage.

competitive_landscape.title: Kernel Spectral Curvature Clustering (KSCC)
competitive_landscape.difference: KSCC kernelizes multiway curvature affinities to linearize nonlinear manifolds; LAPD uses sparse local simplices and path bottlenecks, targeting better scaling and direct small-angle robustness.

competitive_landscape.title: Multi-Manifold Modeling in Non-Euclidean spaces
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. combine sparse coding with tangent and geodesic direction on ambient Riemannian spaces; LAPD assumes Euclidean observations but replaces local tangent estimation with simplex angular paths.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: LAPD is a robust geometric MMC metric with high-probability separation guarantees and a quasi-linear implementation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines a new simplex-angle bottleneck construction, denoising analysis, gap theorem, and broad experiments.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Angle-aware MMC and graph consistency are established themes, but the particular lift to adjacent d-simplices plus infinity-path distance and its gap analysis is a substantive new combination. The most important unresolved boundary is curvature and dimension adaptation.

reviewer_notes: Read all 42 extracted pages, including theorem assumptions/proofs, implementation details, synthetic and real experiments, and appendices. Competitor records were independently checked on arXiv and PMLR on 2026-08-23.
